claim: Negative feedback regulation is the most abundant regulatory motif known to biology.
source: Negative feedback regulation, that is the ability of a gene to repress its own synthesis, is the most abundant regulatory motif known to biology.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific data from this study, drawing on general biological knowledge.

claim: TIER-seq analysis revealed approximately 25,000 RNase E-dependent cleavage sites in Vibrio cholerae.
source: TIER-seq analysis (transiently-inactivating-an-endoribonuclease-followed-by-RNA-seq) revealed ~25,000 RNase E-dependent cleavage sites in Vibrio cholerae
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from TIER-seq analysis performed in this study.

claim: OppZ and CarZ are sRNAs processed from the 3' untranslated region of the oppABCDF and carAB operons, respectively.
source: Focusing on two examples, OppZ and CarZ, we discovered that these sRNAs are processed from the 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) of the oppABCDF and carAB operons, respectively
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including Northern blots and TIER-seq analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: OppZ and CarZ base-pair with their own transcripts to inhibit translation.
source: we discovered that these sRNAs are processed from the 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) of the oppABCDF and carAB operons, respectively, and base-pair with their own transcripts to inhibit translation.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-hybrid predictions, compensatory base-pair exchange experiments, and GFP reporter assays shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: OppZ-mediated autoregulation triggers Rho-dependent transcription termination.
source: For OppZ, this process also triggers Rho-dependent transcription termination.
evidence: This is supported by bicyclomycin (BCM) treatment experiments and Term-Seq analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: sRNAs from 3' UTRs serve as autoregulatory elements allowing negative feedback control at the post-transcriptional level.
source: Our data show that sRNAs from 3' UTRs serve as autoregulatory elements allowing negative feedback control at the post-transcriptional level.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: More than 40% of known transcription factors in E. coli are controlled by negative autoregulation.
source: in Escherichia coli more than 40% of the known transcription factors are controlled by this type of regulation (Rosenfeld et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Rosenfeld et al., 2002.

claim: RNase E is an essential enzyme in E. coli and related bacteria required for ribosome biogenesis and tRNA maturation.
source: Another key factor involved in post-transcriptional gene regulation is ribonuclease E (RNase E), an essential enzyme in E. coli and related bacteria required for ribosome biogenesis and tRNA maturation (Mackie, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mackie, 2013.

claim: The rne-3071 mutation (leucine 68 to phenylalanine) in V. cholerae creates a temperature-sensitive RNase E variant.
source: To study the role of RNase E in this pathogen, we mutated the DNA sequence of the V. cholerae chromosome encoding leucine 68 of RNase E to phenylalanine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This mutation is analogous to the originally described N3071 rneTS isolate of E. coli (Apirion and Lassar, 1978) and exhibits full RNase E activity at permissive temperatures (30°C), but is rendered inactive under non-permissive temperatures (44°C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental validation using Northern blots showing accumulation of RNase E substrates at non-permissive temperature (Figure 1A).

claim: Transfer of the rneTS strain to 44°C led to accumulation of the 9S precursor rRNA.
source: For both RNAs, transfer of the wild-type strain to 44°C only mildly effected their expression, whereas the equivalent procedure performed with the rneTS strain led to the accumulation of the 9S precursor and the full-length MicX transcript (Figure 1A, lanes 1–2 vs. 3–4).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A Northern blot data.

claim: Transfer of the rneTS strain to 44°C led to accumulation of full-length MicX transcript.
source: For both RNAs, transfer of the wild-type strain to 44°C only mildly effected their expression, whereas the equivalent procedure performed with the rneTS strain led to the accumulation of the 9S precursor and the full-length MicX transcript (Figure 1A, lanes 1–2 vs. 3–4).
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1A Northern blot data.

claim: 24,962 RNase E-specific cleavage sites were identified in V. cholerae at 44°C.
source: Comparison of the 5' ends detected in wild-type and rneTS at 30°C showed almost no difference between the two strains (Pearson correlation coefficients R2 ranging from 0.82 to 0.99 depending on the compared replicates), whereas the same analysis at 44°C revealed 24,962 depleted sites in the rneTS strain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is based on TIER-seq data analysis comparing wild-type and rneTS strains.

claim: RNase E cleavage sites occur with a frequency of 2.8 (median)/6.3 (mean) sites per kb in V. cholerae.
source: We discovered that RNase E cleavage sites occur with a frequency of 2.8 (median)/6.3 (mean) sites per kb (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is calculated from the TIER-seq data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The majority of RNase E cleavage events (~69.1%) occurs in coding sequences.
source: The majority of cleavage events occurs in coding sequences (~69.1%), followed by 5' UTRs (~8.4%), antisense RNAs (~7.1%), 3' UTRs (~5.3%), intergenic regions (~4.0%), and sRNAs (~0.6%) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on classification of TIER-seq identified cleavage sites shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The RNase E consensus motif in V. cholerae is 'RN↓WUU'.
source: Together, these data allowed us to determine a consensus motif for RNase E in V. cholerae (Figure 1D). This 5-nt sequence, i.e. 'RN↓WUU'
evidence: This motif was determined from analysis of all detected cleavage sites and is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The RNase E consensus motif in V. cholerae is highly similar to previously determined RNase E motifs of Salmonella enterica and Rhodobacter sphaeroides.
source: This 5-nt sequence, i.e. 'RN↓WUU', is highly similar to previously determined RNase E motifs of Salmonella enterica (Chao et al., 2017) and Rhodobacter sphaeroides (Förstner et al., 2018)
evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and cited previous studies.

claim: RNase E operates by a conserved mechanism of recognition and cleavage across bacterial species.
source: This 5-nt sequence, i.e. 'RN↓WUU', is highly similar to previously determined RNase E motifs of Salmonella enterica (Chao et al., 2017) and Rhodobacter sphaeroides (Förstner et al., 2018), indicating that RNase E operates by a conserved mechanism of recognition and cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of RNase E motifs across different bacterial species.

claim: 17 candidate 3' UTR-derived sRNAs in V. cholerae show potential RNase E-dependent maturation.
source: To analyse which of these sRNAs depend on RNase E for maturation, we searched for RNase E-cleavage sites matching with the first three bases of the annotated sRNAs. 17 sRNAs revealed potential RNase E-dependent maturation (Supplementary file 2A)
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of TIER-seq data matched with annotated sRNAs.

claim: 9 sRNAs (Vcr016, Vcr041, Vcr044, Vcr045, Vcr053, Vcr064, FarS, Vcr079, and Vcr084) were confirmed by Northern blot to depend on RNase E for maturation.
source: using Northern blot analyses of wild-type and rneTS samples, we were able to confirm these results for 9 sRNAs (Vcr016, Vcr041, Vcr044, Vcr045, Vcr053, Vcr064, FarS, Vcr079, and Vcr084; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is confirmed by Northern blot experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: OppZ is 52 base pairs long.
source: The oppZ gene is 52 bps long and conserved among the Vibrios (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the alignment in Figure 2A.

claim: OppZ is conserved among the Vibrios.
source: The oppZ gene is 52 bps long and conserved among the Vibrios (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 2A.

claim: RNase E-mediated cleavage of oppABCDF occurs immediately downstream of the oppF stop codon.
source: RNase E-mediated cleavage of oppABCDF occurs immediately downstream of the oppF stop codon
evidence: This is shown by TIER-seq data and validated by Northern blot in Figure 2B.

claim: OppZ expression coincides with the expression of OppA and OppB proteins.
source: Northern and Western blot analysis of a V. cholerae strain carrying a 3XFLAG epitope at the C-terminus of the chromosomal oppA and oppB genes revealed that OppZ expression coincided with the expression of both proteins (Figure 2C, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is shown by Western and Northern blot data in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of oppABCDF is controlled by a single promoter located approximately 120 bps upstream of oppA.
source: Previous transcriptome data showed that expression of oppABCDF is controlled by a single promotor located ~120 bps upstream of oppA (Papenfort et al., 2015b)
evidence: This is based on previously published transcriptome data.

claim: OppZ is co-expressed with all five opp genes from a single promoter.
source: In contrast, activation of the pBAD promoter led to a significant increase in OppA/B and OppZ (Figure 2C, lanes 11–12), indicating that expression of the oppABCDF-oppZ operon is indeed controlled by a single promoter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by promoter replacement experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: OppZ is efficiently clipped off from a precursor transcript containing oppF-oppZ.
source: Expression of mature OppZ was readily detected from the precursor (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, lane 1 vs. 4) and the size of the processed OppZ transcript was comparable to endogenously expressed OppZ (lane 1) and OppZ transcribed directly by the PTac promoter (lane 3).
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: OppZ binds Hfq in vivo.
source: Indeed, stability experiments using rifampicin-treated V. cholerae showed that OppZ half-life is reduced in Δhfq cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and RNA co-immunoprecipitation experiments of chromosomal Hfq::3XFLAG revealed that OppZ interacts with Hfq in vivo (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: OppZ half-life is reduced in Δhfq cells.
source: Indeed, stability experiments using rifampicin-treated V. cholerae showed that OppZ half-life is reduced in Δhfq cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is shown by stability experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: OppZ is an Hfq-dependent sRNA.
source: Together, these data show that OppZ is an Hfq-dependent sRNA that is processed from the 3' UTR of the polycistronic oppABCDF mRNA by RNase E.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple experiments including co-IP and stability assays.

claim: OppZ over-expression results in approximately 30-fold increase in OppZ levels.
source: Induction of the pBAD promoter for 15 min resulted in a strong increase in OppZ levels (~30 fold, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: OppZ over-expression represses oppBCDF genes.
source: RNA-seq experiments of the corresponding samples revealed four repressed genes (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). Interestingly, these genes were oppBCDF, i.e. the same transcript that OppZ is processed from.
evidence: This is shown by RNA-seq data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: OppZ does not affect oppA expression.
source: We validated OppZ-mediated repression of all four genes using qRT-PCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), which also confirmed that the first gene of the operon, oppA, is not affected by OppZ.
evidence: This is confirmed by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: OppZ over-expression does not reduce the stability of the oppB messenger.
source: Despite the reduced transcript levels of oppBCDF, OppZ over-expression did not reduce the stability of the oppB messenger (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown by transcript stability experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: OppZ forms an RNA duplex with the oppB translation initiation site.
source: Using the RNA-hybrid algorithm (Rehmsmeier et al., 2004), we were able to predict RNA duplex formation of the oppB translation initiation site with the 5' end of the OppZ sRNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is predicted by RNA-hybrid algorithm and validated by compensatory base-pair exchange experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: OppZ represses GFP expression from an oppB::gfp reporter by approximately 7-fold.
source: Transfer of this plasmid into E. coli and co-transformation of the OppZ over-expression plasmid resulted in strong repression of GFP (~7 fold), while mKate2 levels remained constant.
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence measurements in Figure 3C.

claim: Compensatory mutations in both OppZ and oppB restore regulatory control.
source: Mutation of either OppZ or oppB (mutations M1, see Figure 3B) abrogated regulation of GFP and combination of both mutants restored control (Figure 3C, bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated by compensatory base-pair exchange experiments in Figure 3C.

claim: OppZ-mediated repression of OppB::GFP is strongly reduced in E. coli lacking hfq.
source: In contrast, OppZ-mediated repression of OppB::GFP was strongly reduced in E. coli lacking hfq (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence assays in hfq mutant strains in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: OppZ promotes discoordinate expression of the oppABCDF operon.
source: In all cases, OppZ readily inhibited GFP but did not affect mKate2. These results confirm that OppZ promotes discoordinate expression of the oppABCDF operon.
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter assays with different operon fragments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: OppZ expressed from the 3' UTR of gfp inhibits GFP expression.
source: Northern blot analysis revealed that OppZ was efficiently clipped off from the gfp transcript in this construct and fluorescence measurements showed that OppZ also inhibited GFP expression (Figure 3D, bottom, lane 1 vs. 2).
evidence: This is shown by single-plasmid reporter assays in Figure 3D.

claim: Mutation of the RNase E recognition site in oppZ blocks OppZ maturation and abolishes OppB::GFP repression.
source: In addition, mutation of the RNase E recognition site in oppZ (UU→GG, mutation M2; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A) blocked OppZ maturation and abolished OppB::GFP repression (Figure 3D, lane 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: OppZ autoregulation requires RNase E-dependent maturation followed by Hfq-dependent base-pairing, not long-distance intramolecular base-pairing.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that OppZ down-regulates protein synthesis from its own cistron. Furthermore, mutation M2 shows that this autoregulation is not mediated by long-distance intramolecular base-pairing of OppZ with the oppB 5' UTR, but rather requires RNase E-dependent maturation of the transcript followed by Hfq-dependent base-pairing.
evidence: This is inferred from the M2 mutation experiments and other data showing the requirement for RNase E processing and Hfq.

claim: Regulator OppZ inhibits OppB::3XFLAG production but does not affect OppA::3XFLAG levels.
source: when tested in V. cholerae, over-expression of regulator OppZ inhibited OppB::3XFLAG production, but did not affect OppA::3XFLAG levels (Figure 4B, left).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Regulator OppZ reduces the expression of native OppZ.
source: Importantly, regulator OppZ also reduced the expression of native OppZ (Figure 4B, right)
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Introduction of the M1 mutation in regulator OppZ abrogates its effect on native OppZ expression.
source: introduction of the M1 mutation (see Figure 3B) in regulator OppZ abrogated this effect.
evidence: This is shown by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 4B.

claim: OppZ exerts autoregulation of its own transcript.
source: These results revealed that OppZ also exerts autoregulation of its own transcript.
evidence: This is concluded from the regulator OppZ experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutation of the oppB start codon to ATC nullifies OppB::3XFLAG production.
source: As expected, mutation of the oppB start codon had no effect on OppA::3XFLAG levels, but nullified OppB::3XFLAG production (Figure 4C, top).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: Lack of oppB translation results in a strong decrease in OppZ levels.
source: Lack of oppB translation also resulted in a strong decrease in OppZ levels (Figure 4C, bottom)
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutation of the oppB start codon does not change OppZ stability.
source: however, did not change OppZ stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by stability experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Plasmid-based complementation of OppB::3XFLAG in the oppB start codon mutant fails to restore OppZ expression.
source: In addition, plasmid-based complementation of OppB::3XFLAG in the oppB start codon mutant failed to restore OppZ expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is shown by complementation experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: OppZ production is independent of cellular OppB levels.
source: plasmid-based complementation of OppB::3XFLAG in the oppB start codon mutant failed to restore OppZ expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), showing that OppZ production is independent of the cellular OppB levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation experiment results.

claim: Autorepression of oppBCDF-oppZ occurs by a mechanism involving both translation inhibition and transcription termination.
source: Based on these and the results above, we propose that autorepression of oppBCDF-oppZ must occur by a mechanism involving both translation inhibition, as well as transcription termination.
evidence: This is proposed based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including BCM experiments and oppB start codon mutations.

claim: Bicyclomycin (BCM) specifically inhibits Rho protein.
source: In E. coli, Rho protein accounts for a major fraction of all transcription termination events (Ciampi, 2006) and has previously been associated with the regulatory activity of Hfq-dependent sRNAs (Bossi et al., 2012; Sedlyarova et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015). Rho is specifically inhibited by bicyclomycin (BCM; Zwiefka et al., 1993)
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from previous literature.

claim: BCM has no effect on OppZ synthesis in wild-type cells.
source: Whereas BCM had no effect on OppZ synthesis in wild-type cells (Figure 5A, lane 1 vs. 2)
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: BCM strongly increases OppZ and oppBCDF expression in the absence of oppB translation.
source: it strongly increased OppZ and oppBCDF expression in the absence of oppB translation (Figure 5A, lane 3 vs. 4, and Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot and qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Lack of oppB translation down-regulates the expression of oppBCDF-oppZ, while presence of BCM suppresses this effect.
source: Detailed inspection of transcript coverage at the oppABCDF-oppZ genomic locus showed that lack of oppB translation down-regulated the expression of oppBCDF-oppZ, while presence of BCM suppressed this effect (Figure 5C and Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: This is shown by Term-Seq analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Inhibition of oppBCDF mRNA and OppZ by over-expression of regulator OppZ is suppressed in the presence of BCM.
source: Similarly, inhibition of the oppBCDF mRNA and OppZ by over-expression of regulator OppZ (see Figure 4A) was suppressed in the presence of BCM, whereas OppB protein levels remained low presumably due to continued repression of oppB translation initiation by OppZ (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot, Northern blot, and qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 5D–E.

claim: Mutation of the oppB start codon results in strongly decreased OppZ levels.
source: In accordance with the data presented in Figure 4C, mutation of the oppB start codon resulted in strongly decreased OppZ levels (Figure 6B, lane 1 vs. 2)
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: STOP mutations at codons 2, 15, and 65 of oppB result in decreased OppZ levels.
source: we observed similar results when the STOP mutation was introduced at the 2nd, 15th, and 65th codon of oppB (Figure 6B, lanes 3–5).
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: A STOP mutation at codon 115 of oppB leads to increased OppZ expression.
source: In contrast, a STOP mutation at codon 115 led to increased OppZ expression (lane 6)
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: OppZ levels are fully restored when the STOP is placed at codon 215 of oppB.
source: and OppZ levels were fully restored when the STOP was placed at codon 215 of oppB (lane 7).
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Mutation of the oppC, oppD, and oppF start codons has no effect on OppZ production.
source: Likewise, mutation of the oppC, oppD, and oppF start codons had no effect on OppZ production (Figure 6B, lanes 8–10).
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Autorepression of oppBCDF-oppZ relies on inhibition of oppB translation initiation by OppZ, which triggers Rho-dependent transcription termination in the distal part of the oppB sequence.
source: To summarize, our data indicate that autorepression of the oppBCDF-oppZ genes relies on inhibition of oppB translation initiation by OppZ, which triggers Rho-dependent transcription termination in the distal part of the oppB sequence.
evidence: This is concluded from the STOP codon mutagenesis experiments and BCM treatment data.

claim: CarZ (Vcr084) is located in the 3' UTR of the carAB operon.
source: To this end, we searched for potential base-pairing sequences between the sRNAs and the translation initiation regions of their associated genes using the RNA-hybrid algorithm (Rehmsmeier et al., 2004). Indeed, we were able to predict stable RNA duplex formation between the Vcr084 sRNA (located in the 3' UTR of the carAB operon; encoding carbamoyl phosphate synthetase) and the 5' UTR of carA
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CarZ forms a stable RNA duplex with the 5' UTR of carA.
source: Indeed, we were able to predict stable RNA duplex formation between the Vcr084 sRNA (located in the 3' UTR of the carAB operon; encoding carbamoyl phosphate synthetase) and the 5' UTR of carA, which is the first gene of the operon (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is predicted by RNA-hybrid and validated by compensatory base-pair exchange experiments.

claim: Plasmid-borne expression of CarZ strongly inhibits GFP production from carA::gfp and carAB::gfp reporters in E. coli.
source: Plasmid-borne expression of CarZ strongly inhibited GFP production from carA::gfp and carAB::gfp reporters in E. coli (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence assays in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: CarZ binds Hfq in vivo.
source: CarZ binds Hfq in vivo (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Repression of carA::gfp by CarZ requires Hfq.
source: and repression of carA::gfp by CarZ requires Hfq, possibly due to reduced CarZ levels in the hfq mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is shown by experiments in hfq mutant strains in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Transcription of carAB-carZ is controlled by a single promoter located upstream of carA.
source: Transcription of carAB-carZ is controlled by a single promoter located upstream of carA and the three genes are co-expressed in vivo (Figure 7D and Papenfort et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is shown by promoter replacement experiments in Figure 7D and cited from previous work.

claim: CarZ inhibits CarA and CarB protein expression.
source: These results suggested that CarZ provides feedback regulation and using an experimental strategy analogous to Figure 4A, we were able to show that CarZ inhibits CarA and CarB protein expression as well as its own synthesis (Figure 7B,E).
evidence: This is shown by Western and Northern blot analysis in Figure 7E.

claim: CarZ inhibits its own synthesis.
source: we were able to show that CarZ inhibits CarA and CarB protein expression as well as its own synthesis (Figure 7B,E).
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 7E.

claim: Introduction of a STOP codon at the 2nd codon of carA abrogates CarZ expression.
source: Furthermore, introduction of a STOP codon at the 2nd codon of the chromosomal carA gene abrogated CarZ expression
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 7F.

claim: Introduction of a STOP codon at the 2nd codon of carB abrogates CarZ expression.
source: and similar results were obtained when the STOP codon was placed at the 2nd codon of carB (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is shown by Northern blot analysis in Figure 7F.

claim: Inactivation of carA translation blocks CarB production.
source: Of note, inactivation of carA translation also blocked CarB production indicating, among other possibilities, that translation of the two ORFs might be coupled
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 7F.

claim: Expression of CarZ relies on active translation of both carA and carB ORFs.
source: inactivation of carA translation also blocked CarB production indicating, among other possibilities, that translation of the two ORFs might be coupled and that expression of CarZ relies on active translation of both ORFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the STOP codon mutagenesis experiments in Figure 7F.

claim: CarZ is an autoregulatory sRNA.
source: Together, these results provide evidence that CarZ is an autoregulatory sRNA
evidence: This is concluded from multiple experiments showing CarZ regulates its own operon.

claim: Autoregulation by 3' UTR-derived sRNAs might be widespread among this class of sRNAs.
source: and suggest that this function might be more wide-spread among the growing class of 3' UTR-derived sRNAs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the identification of two examples (OppZ and CarZ) and bioinformatic predictions for other sRNAs.

claim: OppZ deficiency results in a moderate increase in OppB expression (approximately 1.8-fold).
source: Quantification of the results revealed a moderate increase in OppB expression (~1.8 fold) in cells lacking oppZ
evidence: This is shown by Western blot quantification in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: OppZ over-expression results in approximately 5-fold decreased OppB levels.
source: Quantification of the results revealed a moderate increase in OppB expression (~1.8 fold) in cells lacking oppZ and ~5 fold decreased OppB levels when OppZ was over-expressed.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot quantification in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither lack of oppZ nor OppZ over-expression significantly affects OppA production.
source: Neither lack of oppZ, nor OppZ over-expression significantly affected OppA production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: OppA protein accumulates equally in wild-type and oppZ mutants after induction.
source: Whereas OppA protein accumulated equally in wild-type and oppZ mutants (Figure 8B)
evidence: This is shown by Western blot quantification in Figure 8B.

claim: Expression of OppB is significantly increased in ΔoppZ cells after induction.
source: expression of OppB was significantly increased in ΔoppZ cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot quantification in Figure 8C.

claim: The OppB response time is approximately 52 minutes in wild-type cells.
source: Calculation of the OppB response time (50% of the maximal expression value) showed a significant delay in ΔoppZ cells (~78 min), when compared to the wild-type control (~52 min).
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The OppB response time is approximately 78 minutes in ΔoppZ cells.
source: Calculation of the OppB response time (50% of the maximal expression value) showed a significant delay in ΔoppZ cells (~78 min), when compared to the wild-type control (~52 min).
evidence: This is calculated from the kinetic data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Autoregulatory sRNAs change the dynamics of their associated genes.
source: We therefore conclude that alike transcription factors, autoregulatory sRNAs change the dynamics of their associated genes
evidence: This is concluded from the kinetic experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: In contrast to transcription factors, autoregulatory sRNAs act at the post-transcriptional level and can direct effects towards specific subgroups of genes within an operon.
source: however, in contrast to transcription factors, sRNAs act at the post-transcriptional level and can direct this effect towards a specific subgroup of genes within an operon.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that OppZ affects oppBCDF but not oppA.

claim: The oppABCDF genes encode an ABC transporter allowing high affinity oligopeptide uptake.
source: The oppABCDF genes encode an ABC transporter allowing high affinity oligopeptide uptake (Hiles et al., 1987).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: OppBCDF constitute the membrane-bound, structural components of the Opp transport system.
source: OppBCDF constitute the membrane-bound, structural components of the transport system, whereas OppA functions as a periplasmic binding protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporter structure.

claim: OppA functions as a periplasmic binding protein.
source: OppBCDF constitute the membrane-bound, structural components of the transport system, whereas OppA functions as a periplasmic binding protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporter structure.

claim: The overall structure of the Opp transporter requires one unit each of OppB, OppC, OppD, and OppF.
source: The overall structure of the transporter requires each one unit of OppB, OppC, OppD, and OppF, while OppA does constitutively interact with the complex and typically accumulates to higher concentrations in the periplasm (Doeven et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: OppA typically accumulates to higher concentrations in the periplasm than the other Opp components.
source: The overall structure of the transporter requires each one unit of OppB, OppC, OppD, and OppF, while OppA does constitutively interact with the complex and typically accumulates to higher concentrations in the periplasm (Doeven et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The carAB genes encode carbamoyl phosphate synthetase.
source: The carAB genes, which are repressed by CarZ, encode carbamoyl phosphate synthetase; an enzyme complex catalyzing the first step in the separate biosynthetic pathways for the production of arginine, and pyrimidine nucleotides (Castellana et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase catalyzes the first step in the biosynthetic pathways for arginine and pyrimidine nucleotides.
source: The carAB genes, which are repressed by CarZ, encode carbamoyl phosphate synthetase; an enzyme complex catalyzing the first step in the separate biosynthetic pathways for the production of arginine, and pyrimidine nucleotides (Castellana et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The CarAB complex contains one subunit of CarA and one subunit of CarB.
source: Similar to OppBCDF, the CarAB complex contains one subunit of CarA and one subunit of CarB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CarAB enzyme complex structure.

claim: Transcriptional control of carAB is complex and controlled by several transcription factors integrating information from purine, pyrimidine, and arginine pathways.
source: Transcriptional control of carAB is complex and controlled by several transcription factors integrating information from purine, pyrimidine, and arginine pathways (Charlier et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Both OppZ and CarZ are efficiently clipped off from foreign genes such as gfp.
source: However, these sRNAs were produced from separate genes and therefore required additional transcriptional input, which increases noise. In contrast, the autoregulatory sRNAs presented here are produced by ribonucleolytic cleavage and we have shown that both OppZ and CarZ are efficiently clipped off from foreign genes, such as gfp (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown by experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 7C.

claim: Autoregulatory sRNAs can be attached to the 3' UTR of other genes to introduce autoregulation into a biological system.
source: We therefore propose that autoregulatory sRNAs can be attached to the 3' UTR of other genes as well, offering a simple and highly modular concept to introduce autoregulation into a biological system.
evidence: This is proposed based on the demonstrated portability of OppZ and CarZ to foreign genes.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses have revealed thousands of stable 3′ UTR RNA tails derived from human transcripts.
source: Given that transcriptomic analyses have revealed thousands of stable 3′ UTR RNA tails derived from human transcripts (Gruber and Zavolan, 2019; Malka et al., 2017)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: RNA-based gene autoregulation could be present and find applications in higher organisms.
source: Given that transcriptomic analyses have revealed thousands of stable 3′ UTR RNA tails derived from human transcripts (Gruber and Zavolan, 2019; Malka et al., 2017), we believe that RNA-based gene autoregulation also could be present and find applications in higher organisms.
evidence: This is speculated based on the existence of 3' UTR-derived RNAs in humans and the findings in bacteria.

claim: RNase E cleavage sites are slightly enriched around start and stop codons of mRNAs.
source: RNase E sites were slightly enriched around start and stop codons of mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is shown by analysis of TIER-seq data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: RNase E cleavage coincides with an increase in AU-content.
source: Furthermore, cleavage coincided with an increase in AU-content (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This is shown by analysis of sequences around cleavage sites in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: RNase E cleavage coincides with a rise in minimal folding energies, suggesting reduced secondary structure around RNase E sites.
source: and a rise in minimal folding energies (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting reduced secondary structure around RNase E sites.
evidence: This is shown by MFE analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and inferred from the data.

claim: Approximately 187 million reads were obtained from twelve TIER-seq samples.
source: We obtained ~187 million reads from the twelve samples (corresponding to three biological replicates of each strain and condition; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is reported from the sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Approximately 98 million unique 5' ends map to the V. cholerae genome from TIER-seq.
source: We obtained ~187 million reads from the twelve samples (corresponding to three biological replicates of each strain and condition; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), resulting in ~98 million unique 5' ends mapping to the V. cholerae genome.
evidence: This is reported from the analysis of sequencing data.

claim: γ-proteobacteria such as V. cholerae do not encode 5' to 3' exoribonucleases.
source: Given that γ-proteobacteria such as V. cholerae do not encode 5' to 3' exoribonucleases (Mohanty and Kushner, 2018)
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: 44 candidate sRNAs located in the 3' UTR of mRNAs were previously annotated in V. cholerae.
source: In V. cholerae, we previously annotated 44 candidate sRNAs located in the 3' UTR of mRNAs (Papenfort et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: Over-expression of CarZ results in accelerated ribonucleolytic decay of the carAB transcript.
source: In contrast, analogous experiments testing the stability of the carA and carB transcripts upon CarZ over-expression revealed a significant drop in transcript stability for both mRNAs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B). These results suggest that translation inhibition of carA by CarZ has two outcomes: 1st) accelerated ribonucleolytic decay of the carAB transcript and 2nd) Rho-mediated transcription termination.
evidence: This is shown by transcript stability experiments in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: CarZ-mediated repression of carA::gfp is approximately 10-fold.
source: Using two regulatory mechanisms (CarZ-carA) instead of one (OppZ-oppB) might explain the strong inhibition of carA::gfp by CarZ (~10 fold, Figure 7C)
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence measurements in Figure 7C.

claim: OppZ-mediated repression of oppB::gfp is approximately 1.8-fold.
source: when compared to the relatively weak repression (1.8-fold) of oppB::gfp by OppZ (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence measurements in Figure 3D.

claim: Rho-dependent termination likely occurs at or close to codon 115 in oppB.
source: Indeed, while our transcriptomic data of the oppB start codon mutant did not allow us to pinpoint the position of the rut site in oppB (Figure 5C), evidence obtained from genetic analyses using various oppB STOP codon mutants revealed that Rho-dependent termination likely occurs at or close to codon 115 in oppB (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is inferred from the STOP codon mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claim: BCM treatment of V. cholerae wild-type cells revealed 699 differentially regulated genes (549 upregulated and 150 repressed genes).
source: BCM treatment of V. cholerae wild-type cells revealed 699 differentially regulated genes (549 upregulated and 150 repressed genes; Supplementary file 3A)
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq analysis of BCM-treated cells.

claim: Rho plays an equally global role in V. cholerae as in E. coli where it accounts for 25-30% of transcription termination events.
source: Approximately 25–30% of all genes in E. coli depend on Rho for transcription termination (Cardinale et al., 2008; Dar and Sorek, 2018b; Peters et al., 2012). BCM treatment of V. cholerae wild-type cells revealed 699 differentially regulated genes (549 upregulated and 150 repressed genes; Supplementary file 3A), suggesting an equally global role for Rho in this organism.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the number of Rho-dependent genes in E. coli (from citations) with BCM-responsive genes in V. cholerae (from this study's data).
